review_note: Align with the lecture’s distinction between research and the recovery-hours estimate. Keep the ledger and short spending-rule slides; remove repeated self-praise and invented predictions from speaker notes.

edits.before: Part II starts here. **You now know enough to run parts of it on purpose** --- which means the question stops being "how does this work" and becomes "what does running it cost me".
edits.after: This week asks what those subroutines cost you to run.
edits.reason: Make the transition concise and avoid claiming that Part II begins in week 6 when repair already began that phase.

edits.before: - This is the hinge of the whole course. Mark it as one.
edits.after: - Ask them to keep one subroutine from the opening in mind as the ledger takes shape.
edits.reason: Replace a demand to emphasise the course’s structure with a useful teaching cue.

edits.before:
- That last line is theirs, not the course's, and it is blunter than anything this course would presume to write.
- This is why there is no version of this lecture that tells them to stop.
edits.after: - Keep the attribution clear: access and protection are benefits reported by participants.
edits.reason: Let the quoted evidence stand and avoid restating the stance announced two slides earlier.

edits.before: - We read the abstract, so don't name the three factors. Say that out loud again --- they should be sick of hearing it by week 6, which is the point.
edits.after: - We read the abstract, so don't name the three factors. State that limit.
edits.reason: Preserve the evidence boundary without making student frustration part of the teaching objective.

edits.before:
- The masking/compensation split matters: hiding and performing are different work and cost differently. Most people in the room do more of one than the other.
- Ask which they do more of. Don't collect answers; just let them notice.
edits.after: - Ask whether they recognise hiding a response, performing an expected one, or both. Does either cost them more? Keep answers private.
edits.reason: Ask about the room’s experience without predicting its distribution or costs.

edits.before:
- This ledger is denominated in recovery hours. That was a guess when it was written. It is the right axis.
- Be honest that the course got lucky here, and that the guess is now a citation.
edits.after: - Recovery hours remain a planning device. Time spent camouflaging and time needed to recover are different quantities; the study gives no conversion between them.
edits.reason: Align with the lecture and remove the unsupported claim that a citation validates the ledger’s unit.

edits.before: Their lay summary goes further than this course ever has: reducing the pressure to camouflage "could benefit everyone in society".
edits.after: Their lay summary adds that reducing the pressure to camouflage "could benefit everyone in society".
edits.reason: Keep the authors’ claim without making the course’s bravery the subject.

edits.before: - That is the pressure column, sourced. And the last line is the mixed-room thesis in the authors' words rather than the course's.
edits.after: - Connect the reported pressure to the ledger: chosen, expected or enforced.
edits.reason: Use the note to connect evidence to an action instead of congratulating the thesis.

edits.before:
- Most pairs disagree on the cost of the same subroutine by a factor of two or more.
- That disagreement IS the week. Land the debrief on it rather than on anyone's number being right.
edits.after: - Ask how close the estimates were and what might account for any difference. Do not treat agreement or disagreement as the expected result.
edits.reason: Align the debrief with the lecture’s open question and remove a fabricated numerical result.

edits.before:
- So the whole room runs some managed performance. What differs is the price.
- Same subroutine, one whole tutorial of eye contact: almost nothing for one person, the rest of the afternoon for another. Neither price is the correct one.
edits.after:
- Managed performance occurs across diagnostic groups; do not assume a particular cost from someone's diagnosis.
- Eye contact is an example: it might cost one person almost nothing and another the rest of the afternoon. The lab asks for their own estimates.
edits.reason: Keep the mixed-room comparison as an example rather than a prediction about every student.

edits.before: That is about as direct as evidence for this section gets.
edits.reason: Cut the narrator’s endorsement after the research result.

edits.before: - Deliberate callback, and the reason that slide was parked rather than spent.
edits.after: - Refer back to the earlier CAT-Q slide if anyone needs the sample or measurement details.
edits.reason: Replace commentary about the slide’s clever construction with a practical teaching cue.

edits.before: The ledger's job is to turn a thing that happens to you into a thing you decide.
edits.after: The pressure column records where that choice is constrained.
edits.reason: Avoid promising full control immediately after teaching that choice can be constrained.

edits.before:
A day you can **see coming** is cheaper than one you meet cold.

```notes
- This is the cheapest intervention in the whole course and almost nobody does it.
edits.after:
Use the estimate to decide **what can move** before the day starts.

```notes
- Use a timetable example: which optional commitment could move if the estimate exceeds the time available?
edits.reason: Give a concrete use for planning instead of promising lower costs or inventing how few students plan.

edits.before:
- Some people will find the decline is cheaper than the run. That is the useful outcome and it surprises them.
- Others will find it genuinely isn't, and that is not a failure --- it is a priced decision, which is the whole skill.
edits.after: - Compare the two estimates without rewarding either choice. Ask what each option buys and what pressure limits the choice.
edits.reason: Do not script the students’ reactions or imply that declining is the desirable result.

edits.before: - This follows straight from Cage & Troxell-Whitman. It is also the least obvious advice in the week.
edits.after: - This is a planning option prompted by the switching association, not an intervention tested by that study.
edits.reason: Keep the advice’s research connection at the strength the study supports.

edits.before: - Say this before the assignment slide, or half the room will hand in a ledger that performs frugality.
edits.after: - Remind them that a low total does not earn a better mark.
edits.reason: Retain the useful assessment clarification without inventing a reaction from half the class.

edits.before:
A row from the ledger you just wrote is the best possible candidate: you already know what it costs and what it buys.

```notes
- Point at their own sheet. Half the room has already chosen without realising.
edits.after:
A row from the ledger is one possible candidate: you have already considered what it costs and what it buys.

```notes
- Invite them to check whether a row gives them a subroutine they can specify and test.
edits.reason: Avoid overselling one route or claiming to know which students have already chosen.

edits.before: - **recovery hours** --- the planning unit, and the axis the research points at
edits.after: - **recovery hours** --- the course's planning unit, estimated from your own experience
edits.reason: Keep the vocabulary recap consistent with the distinction between exposure time and recovery time.

- almost nothing for one person
- the rest of the afternoon for another

edits.after:
Sustained eye contact for one whole tutorial might cost:

- almost nothing for one person
- the rest of the afternoon for another

**Neither person's estimate sets the price for the other.**

Thursday's lab compares your estimates.

- Keep this as an example. Let the lab establish which costs vary in this room.
